Build a trial in which exposure has **exactly no effect** on outcome, run the
exposure–response analysis anyone would run, and watch it report a large,
tightly bounded, entirely false effect. Then find the diagnostic that exposes it.

Everything here is simulated, and every true parameter is written down before
the analysis sees the data. That is the point: on real data you cannot check
your answer against the truth, so the only place to learn what these analyses
do is somewhere the truth is known.

Nothing beyond NumPy and Matplotlib.

::: {#33779d7d .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

INK, MUTED, GRID = "#3A464E", "#66737C", "#DFE5E8"
DRUG, PROGNOSIS  = "#2A5DB0", "#A32C42"
```
:::


## The generative model

Six lines of pharmacology, and one line that is the whole lesson.

Antibody clearance rises with catabolic burden — the sicker the patient, the
faster the drug goes away. Sicker patients also die sooner, for reasons that
have nothing to do with the drug. Those two facts alone are enough.

::: {#5fb89df1 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def simulate(seed=20260910, n=1200, theta_cl=0.40, beta_s=0.55,
             true_te=0.70, beta_exp=0.00, proxy_sd=0.50):
    """theta_cl  severity -> clearance   (catabolism)
       beta_s    severity -> hazard      (prognosis)
       true_te   the drug's real effect  (hazard ratio vs no drug)
       beta_exp  exposure -> hazard      (THE ANSWER; 0.00 means none)
       proxy_sd  how badly the recorded covariate measures true severity"""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    CL0, TAU, DOSE, H0, TMAX = 0.25, 14.0, 240.0, 0.020, 36.0

    def arm(treated):
        S    = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                       # true severity, never observed
        X    = S + rng.normal(0, proxy_sd, n)            # what the case report form records
        CL   = CL0 * np.exp(theta_cl * S + rng.normal(0, 0.25, n))
        cavg = DOSE / (CL * TAU)                         # exposure falls as clearance rises
        h    = (H0
                * np.exp(beta_s * S)                     # prognosis drives the hazard
                * (true_te if treated else 1.0)          # the drug works, by a fixed amount
                * np.exp(beta_exp * np.log(cavg / np.median(cavg))))
        t = rng.exponential(1.0 / h)
        return dict(S=S, X=X, CL=CL, cavg=cavg,
                    time=np.minimum(t, TMAX), event=t <= TMAX)

    return arm(True), arm(False)

treated, control = simulate()
print(f"treated {len(treated['time'])}, control {len(control['time'])}")
print(f"events:  {treated['event'].sum()} vs {control['event'].sum()}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
treated 1200, control 1200
events:  504 vs 626
```
:::
:::


Exposure enters the hazard through `beta_exp` and nothing else. At `0.00` the
term is `exp(0 · log(...)) = 1` for every patient, so exposure is arithmetically
absent from every survival time in the dataset.

::: {#9a863fcb .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# The parameter has to be live, or "we set it to zero" proves nothing.
# Give exposure a real effect and the survival times must change.
same    = simulate(beta_exp=0.00)[0]
with_er = simulate(beta_exp=-0.50)[0]
assert np.array_equal(same["cavg"], with_er["cavg"]), "same patients, same exposures"
assert not np.array_equal(same["time"], with_er["time"]), \
    "beta_exp must reach the survival times, or setting it to 0 means nothing"
print(f"beta_exp = 0.00  ->  exposure multiplier is exactly 1 for all "
      f"{len(same['time'])} patients")
print("true exposure effect per e-fold of Cavg: HR = 1.000000 (by construction)")
```

## The hazard ratio, without an optimiser

For exponential survival the hazard rate is events divided by person-time, and
a hazard ratio is one such rate divided by another. No `coxph`, no solver — and
the arithmetic *is* the definition, which is worth seeing once.

::: {#64c71d5e .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def rate(d, m):
    return d["event"][m].sum(), d["time"][m].sum()

def hazard_ratio(dA, mA, dB, mB):
    eA, tA = rate(dA, mA)
    eB, tB = rate(dB, mB)
    hr = (eA / tA) / (eB / tB)
    se = np.sqrt(1 / eA + 1 / eB)                 # standard error of log HR
    return hr, hr * np.exp(-1.96 * se), hr * np.exp(1.96 * se)

def quartiles(d, key="cavg"):
    q = np.quantile(d[key], [0.25, 0.50, 0.75])
    return [d[key] <= q[0],
            (d[key] > q[0]) & (d[key] <= q[1]),
            (d[key] > q[1]) & (d[key] <= q[2]),
            d[key] > q[2]]

Q = quartiles(treated)
print(f"{'':4s}{'mean Cavg':>11s}{'mean severity':>15s}{'events':>8s}{'hazard':>9s}")
for i, m in enumerate(Q, 1):
    e, pt = rate(treated, m)
    print(f"  Q{i}{treated['cavg'][m].mean():11.1f}"
          f"{treated['S'][m].mean():+15.2f}{e:8d}{e / pt:9.4f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
      mean Cavg  mean severity  events   hazard
  Q1       38.1          +1.12     185   0.0269
  Q2       58.2          +0.30     131   0.0160
  Q3       80.3          -0.25     106   0.0121
  Q4      127.7          -1.07      82   0.0088
```
:::
:::


The exposure quartiles differ in exposure. They also differ, by more than a
standard deviation end to end, in how sick the patients were before anyone
gave them anything.

## 1. The analysis anyone would run

::: {#b9c69f9c .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
naive = hazard_ratio(treated, Q[3], treated, Q[0])
print("highest vs lowest exposure quartile")
print("  HR = {:.2f}   95% CI {:.2f} to {:.2f}".format(*naive))
print("  truth       1.00")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
highest vs lowest exposure quartile
  HR = 0.33   95% CI 0.25 to 0.42
  truth       1.00
```
:::
:::


A 67% reduction in hazard, with a confidence interval nowhere near 1, from a
drug whose exposure does nothing. This is not noise and it will not go away
with a larger trial — more patients would tighten that interval around the
wrong number.

## 2. Adjusting for prognosis does not fix it

The obvious response is to put the prognostic covariate in the model. Here it
is, as a stratified comparison across five strata of the recorded covariate.

::: {#9994d362 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
xq = np.quantile(treated["X"], [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8])
strata = ([treated["X"] <= xq[0]]
          + [(treated["X"] > xq[i]) & (treated["X"] <= xq[i + 1]) for i in range(3)]
          + [treated["X"] > xq[3]])

num = den = 0.0
for s in strata:
    eA, tA = rate(treated, s & Q[3])
    eB, tB = rate(treated, s & Q[0])
    if eA and eB:
        num += eA / tA
        den += eB / tB
print(f"  HR stratified on the recorded covariate = {num / den:.2f}")
print(f"  unadjusted                              = {naive[0]:.2f}")
print( "  truth                                   = 1.00")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
  HR stratified on the recorded covariate = 0.62
  unadjusted                              = 0.33
  truth                                   = 1.00
```
:::
:::


Half the bias, and half is not enough. The covariate you recorded is a noisy
reading of the thing that actually drives both clearance and death, and
adjusting for a noisy proxy removes only the part of the confounding the proxy
managed to capture.

## 3. The diagnostic that works

Stop asking whether high exposure beats low exposure inside the treated arm.
Ask instead whether the **lowest**-exposure patients still beat comparable
patients who never got the drug. If they do, the exposure gradient was never a
gradient in drug effect.

::: {#89c18fc5 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def match_controls(treated, control, mask, on="X"):
    """Nearest-neighbour match, without replacement, on one covariate."""
    pool, chosen = list(range(len(control[on]))), []
    for i in np.where(mask)[0]:
        k = min(range(len(pool)),
                key=lambda k: abs(control[on][pool[k]] - treated[on][i]))
        chosen.append(pool.pop(k))
    m = np.zeros(len(control[on]), bool)
    m[chosen] = True
    return m

mX = match_controls(treated, control, Q[0], on="X")
matched = hazard_ratio(treated, Q[0], control, mX)
print(f"matched on the recorded covariate:  "
      f"treated Q1 mean {treated['X'][Q[0]].mean():+.2f} "
      f"vs controls {control['X'][mX].mean():+.2f}")
print("  HR (lowest-exposure treated vs matched controls) "
      "= {:.2f}   95% CI {:.2f} to {:.2f}".format(*matched))
print("  the drug's true effect                           = 0.70")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
matched on the recorded covariate:  treated Q1 mean +1.15 vs controls +1.13
  HR (lowest-exposure treated vs matched controls) = 0.90   95% CI 0.74 to 1.10
  the drug's true effect                           = 0.70
```
:::
:::


The patients with the least drug exposure still got most of the drug's benefit.
That is incompatible with a real exposure–response and compatible with the
truth, which is that the drug works and the dose is on a plateau.

::: {#4afe1c43 .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
mS = match_controls(treated, control, Q[0], on="S")
oracle = hazard_ratio(treated, Q[0], control, mS)
print("  matched on TRUE severity (not available in life) "
      "= {:.2f}   95% CI {:.2f} to {:.2f}".format(*oracle))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
  matched on TRUE severity (not available in life) = 0.74   95% CI 0.60 to 0.89
```
:::
:::


Matching on the truth recovers 0.70. Matching on what was written down lands
short of it. The gap between those two lines is the price of measuring
prognosis imperfectly, and in a real study nobody can show you that gap.

## The tests, and the sabotage that makes them tests

An assertion that passes whether or not the thing it guards is broken is
decoration. Each check below is paired with a deliberately broken run that must
make it fail.

::: {#checks .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# Sabotage 1: clearance stops tracking prognosis. Nothing else changes.
flat_tr, flat_ct = simulate(theta_cl=0.0)
flat_naive = hazard_ratio(flat_tr, quartiles(flat_tr)[3],
                          flat_tr, quartiles(flat_tr)[0])

# Sabotage 2: the covariate is recorded almost perfectly.
perf_tr, perf_ct = simulate(proxy_sd=0.01)
perf_Q = quartiles(perf_tr)
perf_matched = hazard_ratio(perf_tr, perf_Q[0], perf_ct,
                            match_controls(perf_tr, perf_ct, perf_Q[0], "X"))

checks = [
    ("a zero exposure effect is reported as a large one",
     naive[2] < 0.75),
    ("and it is not a confidence problem — the interval excludes 1",
     naive[2] < 1.0),
    ("removing the clearance-prognosis link removes the whole signal",
     flat_naive[1] < 1.0 < flat_naive[2]),
    ("case-matching moves the estimate most of the way back",
     matched[0] > 2 * naive[0]),
    ("recording prognosis better closes the residual gap",
     abs(perf_matched[0] - oracle[0]) < abs(matched[0] - oracle[0])),
]
for msg, ok in checks:
    print(f"  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {msg}")
assert all(ok for _, ok in checks)
print(f"\n  sabotage 1 (theta_cl = 0):  HR {flat_naive[0]:.2f} "
      f"({flat_naive[1]:.2f}-{flat_naive[2]:.2f})  <- the bias is gone")
print(f"  sabotage 2 (perfect covariate): matched HR {perf_matched[0]:.2f} "
      f"vs {matched[0]:.2f} with a noisy one")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
  PASS  a zero exposure effect is reported as a large one
  PASS  and it is not a confidence problem — the interval excludes 1
  PASS  removing the clearance-prognosis link removes the whole signal
  PASS  case-matching moves the estimate most of the way back
  PASS  recording prognosis better closes the residual gap

  sabotage 1 (theta_cl = 0):  HR 1.01 (0.79-1.30)  <- the bias is gone
  sabotage 2 (perfect covariate): matched HR 0.75 vs 0.90 with a noisy one
```
:::
:::


Sabotage 1 is the important one. Set the clearance–prognosis link to zero and
the spurious effect vanishes completely — which is the proof that the link, and
nothing else in this simulation, produced it.

## What you should take away

An exposure–response analysis inside a single treatment arm is an observational
study wearing a pharmacokinetic costume. Randomisation assigned the dose; it did
not assign the exposure, and whatever determines the exposure is free to
determine the outcome too.
